content: Risk of Bias Assessment Selection Bias Random Sequence Generation: The risk of bias was judged as low. The randomization process was computer-generated and stratified based on baseline C-reactive protein levels (<10 or ≥10 mg/L) and serum ferritin levels (<25 or ≥25 µg/L). Allocation Concealment: The risk of bias was also low. Two investigators, who were not involved in recruitment or data collection, performed the random assignment of participants to groups. Baseline Outcome Measurements Similarity of Baseline Outcome Measurements: The risk of bias was low. There were no statistically significant differences in baseline variables between the groups, ensuring comparability. Similarity of Baseline Characteristics: The risk of bias was low. The children’s age and sex were similar across groups, reducing the likelihood of confounding. Attrition Bias Incomplete Outcome Data: The risk of bias was low. Sixteen children were excluded from the study for various reasons: Eleven children were withdrawn by their parents. Among these: Three children disliked the milk. Two parents were concerned about blood sampling. Two children experienced loose stools without signs of milk intolerance. One child had a urinary tract infection and vesicoureteral reflux. One child had constipation. One child experienced gastroenteritis followed by constipation. One parent refused to feed their child low-fat yogurt. One child was removed due to milk intolerance following gastroenteritis. Three children were excluded for protocol non-adherence. One child was withdrawn after sustaining injuries in a car accident. Performance Bias Blinding of Participants and Personnel: The risk of bias was low. Parents and investigators were blinded to the type of milk provided, and investigators were also blinded to the dairy products used. Contamination: The risk of bias was unclear. There was no clear evidence to determine whether contamination occurred. Detection Bias Blinding of Outcome Assessment: The risk of bias was high. A dietitian, who was aware of the randomization results, controlled the children’s dietary records. However, staff were thoroughly trained in the feeding regimen and instructed parents on how to record their child’s diet. Reporting Bias Selective Reporting: The risk of bias was high. The study was approved by the Ethics Committee at Lund University, Sweden, but the sample size was very small, which may have influenced the reporting of results. Other Bias Recruitment Bias: The risk of bias was unclear and not applicable, as this domain was only evaluated in cluster-randomized studies. Baseline Imbalance: The risk of bias was unclear and not applicable, as this domain was only evaluated in cluster-randomized studies. Loss of Clusters: The risk of bias was unclear and not applicable, as this domain was only evaluated in cluster-randomized studies. Incorrect Analysis: The risk of bias was unclear and not applicable, as this domain was only evaluated in cluster-randomized studies. Compatibility with Individual RCTs: The risk of bias was unclear and not applicable, as this domain was only evaluated in cluster-randomized studies. Study Summaries Szymlek-Gay 2009 Methods: This was a randomized, placebo-controlled trial with three arms. Participants: The study included healthy, non-anemic children aged 12–20 months from urban centers in New Zealand at sea level. Interventions: A total of 225 children were randomly assigned to one of three groups: 1. Daily consumption of 6 mg of iron from red meat dishes. 2. Daily consumption of milk fortified with 5 mg of iron per 100 g. 3. Daily consumption of non-fortified milk containing 0.1 mg of iron per 100 g. Participants in the milk groups replaced their regular milk with either commercially available iron-fortified powdered cow’s milk or non-fortified powdered cow’s milk. Mothers continued breastfeeding at their discretion. The intervention lasted 20 weeks. For this review, only groups 2 and 3 were analyzed. Outcomes: Hemoglobin, serum ferritin, serum transferrin receptor, and C-reactive protein levels were measured. Iron depletion, iron-deficient erythropoiesis, and iron deficiency anemia were assessed, and body iron was calculated. Notes: Fortified milk contained ferrous sulfate, calcium, magnesium, zinc, vitamin C, vitamin E, niacin, vitamin A, vitamin D, vitamin B6, thiamin, and folate. Non-fortified milk was standard whole milk powder with added vitamins A and D. Milk was packaged in identical white cans with concealed codes. The study was funded by the Health Research Council of New Zealand, Meat and Livestock Australia, Meat and Wool New Zealand, and the University of Otago. Van der Gaag 2015 Methods: This was a non-randomized retrospective case-control study. Participants: The study included children aged 1–6 years with recurrent respiratory tract symptoms. Interventions: Ninety-nine children were assigned to one of two groups: 1. Group 1 (n=50) received dietary advice to consume whole milk, yogurt, and natural butter daily. 2. Group 2 (n=49) continued their usual consumption of semi-skimmed milk and low-fat margarine (control group). The intervention lasted two months. Outcomes: Respiratory symptoms were assessed. Notes: The source of funding was not mentioned. Villalpando 2006 Methods: This was a double-blind randomized controlled trial with two arms. Participants: The study included healthy children aged 10–30 months from a peri-urban community near Puebla, Mexico. Participants were selected from a registry maintained by the local health facility. Interventions: A total of 115 children were randomly assigned to one of two groups: 1. Group 1 (n=58) received 400 mL/day of fortified cow’s whole milk. 2. Group 2 (n=57) received 400 mL/day of non-fortified cow’s whole milk. Milk was distributed in powder form, and mothers were instructed on reconstitution. Weekly deliveries ensured the intended daily consumption for infants. Outcomes: Hemoglobin, serum ferritin, soluble transferrin receptors, and C-reactive protein concentrations were measured. The prevalence of anemia was also estimated. Notes: Fortified milk contained 28 mg of zinc (as zinc oxide) and 48 mg of ascorbic acid per 400 mL. Milk packages were indistinguishable except for a color-coded band. The study was supported by the Ministry of Social Development of Mexico and the National Public Health Institute.
